name: Anemia Due to Acute Blood Loss

clinicalPearls: In the first hours after a sudden large bleed the routine blood count typically does NOT reveal anemia, because hemoglobin concentration is initially unchanged; the dominant problem at this stage is hypovolemia, not a low hemoglobin (p.807).

Hemoglobin falls only gradually over several hours to days as the intravascular volume is restored — either by intravenous fluids given acutely, or by the body's own fluid shift from the extravascular into the intravascular compartment (hemodilution) — so the measured hemoglobin lags behind the true blood loss (p.807).
The degree of anemia eventually reflects the amount lost: as a rough guide, a hemoglobin around 7 g/dL after about 3 days implies roughly half of the total blood has been lost (p.807).
If bleeding stops, the marrow response (rising reticulocyte count and erythropoietin) gradually corrects the anemia; this reticulocyte rise mirrors the marrow response seen in hemolysis (p.807).
Acute blood loss and hemolysis are the two principal causes of anemia accompanied by an elevated reticulocyte count (p.807).
Signs of vascular instability appear once roughly 25% or more of total blood volume is lost; donating a unit of blood (~20% of volume) is usually only minimally symptomatic (p.807).

Bedside signs of concealed bleeding include the Grey Turner sign (flank ecchymosis, suggesting retroperitoneal hemorrhage), the Cullen sign (periumbilical ecchymosis, suggesting intraperitoneal or retroperitoneal bleeding), and dullness to chest percussion (suggesting intrapleural blood) (p.807).

The amount of blood lost is frequently overestimated when a scene appears bloody; careful repeated examination and directed investigations (e.g., ultrasound, endoscopy) are needed to localize occult bleeding (p.807).
Whenever hemoglobin drops abruptly, acute posthemorrhagic anemia should be suspected regardless of the history initially offered by the patient (p.807).

Compensation is partly achieved by a rightward shift of the oxygen–hemoglobin dissociation curve: with mild loss via the Bohr effect (lower pH / higher CO2), and in more chronic anemia via rising intracellular 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate, which aids oxygen unloading (p.807).

Surgery is an important iatrogenic cause of acute posthemorrhagic anemia; blood loss can be substantial (e.g., up to about 2 L with radical prostatectomy) and should be measured and monitored (p.807-808).
harrison.pathophysiology: Blood loss produces anemia by two mechanisms: direct loss of red cells, and — if the bleeding is protracted — gradual depletion of iron stores leading to iron-deficiency anemia (the latter covered separately). Acute posthemorrhagic anemia follows the former. Hemorrhage may be external (trauma, obstetric) or internal (gastrointestinal tract, splenic rupture, ruptured ectopic pregnancy, subarachnoid hemorrhage, leaking aneurysm). After a sudden large loss there are three sequential clinical/pathophysiologic stages: (1) hypovolemia dominates and threatens high-flow organs (brain, kidneys), so impaired consciousness and acute renal failure are early dangers, while the blood count still appears normal because hemoglobin concentration is unchanged; (2) baroreceptor and stretch-receptor activation triggers vasopressin and other peptide release and a shift of fluid from the extravascular into the intravascular space, producing hemodilution that converts hypovolemia into measurable anemia proportional to the volume lost; (3) provided bleeding ceases, increased marrow erythropoiesis (reflected by elevated reticulocytes and erythropoietin) gradually ameliorates the anemia. Tissue oxygen delivery is defended by rightward shifts of the oxygen–hemoglobin dissociation curve (acute Bohr effect from lower pH/higher CO2; chronic rise in 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate) and by shunting blood away from organs with relatively rich supply (kidney, gut, skin) (p.807).
additionalDifferentials: Hemolytic anemia (the other major cause of anemia with reticulocytosis) (p.807)
Iron-deficiency anemia from chronic/protracted blood loss (p.807)
Other hypoproliferative or production-failure anemias when reticulocyte count is not elevated (p.807)
nonInfectiousMimics: Hemolysis — also presents as anemia with an elevated reticulocyte count and a brisk marrow response, mimicking the recovery phase of acute blood loss (p.807)
Hypovolemic shock from non-hemorrhagic causes (dehydration, fluid sequestration) can reproduce the early hypovolemic picture before any fall in hemoglobin (p.807)
additionalInvestigations: Serial hemoglobin/hematocrit measurements — recognizing that early values are misleadingly normal and fall over hours as volume is restored (p.807)
Reticulocyte count and erythropoietin level — rise during the marrow recovery phase (p.807)
Imaging or endoscopy (e.g., sonogram, endoscopy) to localize occult internal bleeding (p.807)
Targeted physical examination for signs of concealed hemorrhage (Grey Turner sign, Cullen sign, chest dullness) (p.807)
redFlags: Loss of consciousness or acute renal failure early on, reflecting hypovolemic threat to brain and kidneys before any anemia is detectable (p.807)
Postural hypotension and tachycardia with a preference to remain supine, indicating sudden loss exceeding ~30% of blood volume that overwhelms sympathetic compensation (p.807)
Hypovolemic shock — confusion, dyspnea, diaphoresis, hypotension, tachycardia — indicating loss >40% (>~2 L in an average adult) and significant vital-organ hypoperfusion (p.807)
Tachycardia, tachypnea, narrowed pulse pressure, cold, pale, mottled skin and reduced urine output signaling sympathetic compensation for ongoing loss (p.807)
harrison.prognosis: Outcome depends on the rapidity and volume of loss and on whether the source can be controlled. If bleeding is stopped, the marrow's compensatory rise in red cell production gradually corrects the anemia. The acute danger is not the anemia itself but hypovolemia and impaired organ perfusion: losses above ~30% of blood volume overwhelm normal compensatory mechanisms, and losses >40% (>~2 L in an average adult) produce hypovolemic shock with significant vital-organ perfusion deficits (p.807).
pitfalls: Mistakenly excluding significant hemorrhage because an early blood count shows a normal hemoglobin — the fall is delayed until volume is restored (p.807).
Overestimating blood loss from the bloody appearance of a scene rather than from careful clinical assessment (p.807).
Failing to suspect occult internal bleeding after trauma, where even large losses may not be immediately obvious (p.807).
Focusing on the anemia number rather than on hypovolemia and organ perfusion, which are the true early threats in large acute losses (p.807).
harrison.severityClassification: Severity tracks the fraction of total blood volume lost: ~20% (one unit) is usually minimally symptomatic; signs of vascular instability emerge at ~25% or more; sudden loss of >30% overwhelms sympathetic compensation and produces postural hypotension and tachycardia; loss of >40% (>~2 L in an average-sized adult) causes hypovolemic shock (confusion, dyspnea, diaphoresis, hypotension, tachycardia). Symptomatic chronic/progressive anemia from slower loss often becomes apparent only when hemoglobin falls below ~70-80 g/L (7-8 g/dL), and intrinsic compensation maintains normal tissue oxygen delivery only across about a 20-30 g/L (2-3 g/dL) hemoglobin deficit (p.807).
management: Immediate control of the bleeding source through endoscopic haemostasis, interventional radiological embolisation or surgery as dictated by the site
Restore circulating volume with intravenous crystalloid resuscitation to treat the dominant early threat of hypovolaemia
Red cell transfusion guided by the volume lost and haemodynamic state, with activation of a major haemorrhage protocol for massive loss
Correct coagulopathy and reverse any contributing anticoagulant or antiplatelet agents
Iron replacement once bleeding is controlled to replenish depleted stores and support the reticulocyte-driven marrow recovery
Serial haemoglobin, haematocrit and vital-sign monitoring, recognising that early haemoglobin lags behind true loss until haemodilution occurs
Escalate to critical care for shock, impaired consciousness or acute kidney injury from organ hypoperfusion

flowcharts.title: Diagnosis and management of acute blood loss anaemia

nodes.text: Resuscitate with IV fluid; activate major haemorrhage protocol
Serial Hb and vitals; examine for concealed bleeding
Stop the source: endoscopy, embolisation or surgery
Transfuse red cells; plasma, platelets, cryo for coagulopathy
Iron replacement and monitor reticulocyte recovery
